The answer is straightforward, and it is good news for your research: **there is no birth certificate to find, because one was never created.**

## Why no birth certificate exists

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths in England and Wales did not begin until **1 July 1837**, established by the Registration Act 1836. Your ancestor born around 1820 arrived in the world approximately seventeen years before the government started issuing birth certificates. No certificate was ever produced for this event, so no archive holds one.

## What records DO exist for a birth around 1820 in Dorset

**Anglican parish registers** — These are your first port of call. They record baptisms (not births), marriages, and burials. The baptism entry for a child born around 1820 would typically have been recorded within days or weeks of the actual birth. It will give you the child's name, date of baptism, and parents' names (usually the father's name only, unless the child was illegitimate). For Dorset, these registers are largely held at the Dorset History Centre in Dorchester, and many have been digitized.

**Bishop's transcripts** — These are annual copies of parish registers sent to the diocesan bishop, and they frequently survive even where the original register does not. Dorset fell under the Diocese of Salisbury for much of its history, so these copies may be held separately from the parish originals.

**Nonconformist records** — If your ancestor's family were Methodists, Baptists, Quakers, or another dissenting congregation — and Nonconformity was well established in rural Dorset by the early 1800s — they would have been registered in a chapel register rather than the Church of England. Many of these were deposited with the General Register Office in 1837 and are now held at the National Archives (series RG 4–8).

## One additional complication worth knowing

Even after civil registration began in July 1837, early compliance was poor — many births were never reported to the registrar in the first decades, because enforcement was weak. So the absence of a civil registration record is not proof that someone was born before 1837; it may simply mean their birth was never reported. This means parish records remain essential even for events after 1837.

## The key practical shift

You are not looking for a birth certificate — you are looking for a **baptism entry** in the Church of England (or Nonconformist) registers for the relevant Dorset parish. The baptism record is the original source, and it pre-dates any civil record by centuries.

---

**Next steps:**
1. Identify which Dorset parish your ancestor's family belonged to and search its baptism register
2. If the parish register has a gap around 1820, search the bishop's transcripts (Diocese of Salisbury)
3. If the family had dissenting connections, search Nonconformist registers at the National Archives (RG 4–8)

### The Political and Economic Backdrop

The 1840s mark the peak of one of the largest German emigration waves in the nineteenth century, with two overlapping causes:

The years **1845–1847** brought severe agricultural crises across much of Central Europe — potato crop failures, grain shortfalls, and regional famines, especially in the southwestern German states of **Baden, Württemberg, and the Rhineland-Palatinate**. Pennsylvania already had the largest established German-speaking community in North America, rooted in eighteenth-century immigration from the Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden, and Switzerland — the "Pennsylvania Deutsch" (anglicized to "Pennsylvania Dutch"). Chain migration made Pennsylvania a natural destination: a letter from a cousin already in Lancaster or Berks County was more persuasive than any advertisement. Major ports of entry were **Baltimore** (most common for those heading inland to Pennsylvania) and **New York**, with some arriving via Philadelphia.

If your ancestor's records mention "Dutch" — an enumerator's note, a church description, a neighbor's recollection — this almost certainly means **"Deutsch" (German)**, not from the Netherlands. This linguistic shorthand pervades Pennsylvania records of the period.

For an emigrant leaving around 1845, **there were no centralized German civil birth, marriage, or death records in most regions.** Civil registration varied enormously:

- Rhine provinces (under Napoleonic influence): as early as 1792
- Prussia: not until 1874
- National standard: January 1876

German names were frequently anglicized — either voluntarily or by the enumerator writing what they heard:

|--------|-----------|

The FamilySearch Germany wiki directs researchers to:
- **Landesarchive (state archives)** for surviving Kirchenbücher

- **Archion and Matricula**, online portals for digitized German church records by denomination

## Irish Immigration to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania in the 1840s

### The Push Factor: The Great Famine (1845–1852)

The defining event driving Irish immigration to Schuylkill County in the 1840s was the Great Famine. Roughly one million people died and a million more emigrated from Ireland during the period 1845–1852. Pennsylvania's anthracite coalfields — including Schuylkill, Carbon, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties — became a primary destination for Famine-era arrivals. For research purposes, the timing of arrival within the decade matters: anyone arriving before 1855 (when Castle Garden opened as a formal immigration depot in New York) will appear in pre-Castle Garden **Customs Passenger Lists**.

---

### The Pull Factor: Anthracite Coal

Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 and by the 1830s had become a major center of anthracite coal mining. The region was widely called "Coal Country," and the mines attracted waves of Irish, Welsh, and Eastern European immigrant laborers. Irish workers — many arriving via Philadelphia after the Great Famine — dominated the mining workforce through the 1840s and 1850s.

The population data makes the scale of this immigration strikingly visible. The county grew from **29,053 residents in 1840 to 60,713 in 1850** — more than doubling in a single decade — and then to 89,510 by 1860. This was not natural increase; it was driven overwhelmingly by immigrant labor entering the mines.

---

### How They Arrived: Ports and Passenger Lists

The Steerage Act of 1819 (effective 1820) required ship captains to file a passenger manifest naming **every passenger aboard** — adults, children, and infants alike, each on their own line. For Famine-era Irish immigrants arriving in the 1840s, the most common ports of entry were **Philadelphia** (the nearest major port to Schuylkill County), **New York**, **Baltimore**, and **Boston**.

A critical practical point: because all passengers — including young children — received individual entries on Customs Passenger Lists, researchers should pull the **full manifest page** rather than searching only by an adult's name. Family members traveling together will appear as adjacent entries on the same page. Cholera and typhus outbreaks during the Famine years generated supplementary port health records that can provide additional documentation.

---

### Chain Migration and Ethnic Clustering

Irish immigrants to Schuylkill County followed classic chain-migration patterns: one man would arrive, find work at a colliery, and send word back to family and neighbors, who then followed. This produced concentrations of people from the same Irish parish or townland in the same mining patch or borough — **Pottsville, Minersville, Tamaqua, Shenandoah**, and other mining communities.

This clustering has two direct research implications:
1. **FAN cluster approach**: Neighbors in an Irish mining community were often also relatives or people from the same home locality in Ireland.
2. **Catholic parish records**: The community rapidly established Catholic churches, and their registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — often predate statewide Pennsylvania vital registration (which did not begin until **1906**) by decades.

---

### Occupational and Employer Records

Mining company employment records, where they survive, list worker names, nationalities, and sometimes prior residence. The **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** holds payroll ledgers for several collieries. These are non-governmental records that can fill gaps left by the absence of early civil registration.

---

### The Molly Maguires: A Later But Rich Record Set

The Molly Maguires — a secret society active among Irish miners in Schuylkill County in the 1860s–1870s — generated extensive court records, trial transcripts, depositions, and Pinkerton detective reports that name hundreds of Irish-born miners and their families. While these records postdate the 1840s immigration wave, they document the same community one generation on and can help connect Famine-era immigrants to their children's generation.

---

### Naturalization Records

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — federal, state, or local. For Schuylkill County Irish immigrants, check county court records as well as federal courts in Philadelphia. Naturalization files (declaration of intent and petition for naturalization) routinely state **birthplace, arrival date, port, and sometimes the ship name**, making them a direct bridge back to passenger lists and Irish origins.

The 1840s were the decade when Schuylkill County transformed from a small mining settlement into a boomtown, almost entirely on the backs of Famine-era Irish immigrants who more than doubled the county's population in ten years. The best documentary trail connecting an Irish ancestor to their homeland runs through Customs Passenger Lists, Catholic parish registers in the specific mining community, and pre-1906 county court naturalization files — all actively created during and immediately after this period of intense immigration.

## Patronymic Surnames in Norway

This is one of the most important questions in Norwegian genealogy research, and the patronymic naming system is the key to answering it.

Norwegian surnames were **patronymic** until the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Each generation took a new surname derived from the father's given name:

- A son of **Erik** became **Eriksen** (Erik's son)
- A son of **Per** or **Peder** became **Pedersen** (Peder's son)

These surnames were **not hereditary** — they changed with every generation and do not function like modern fixed family names.

---

## What the Two Surnames Tell You

The difference between **Eriksen** and **Pedersen** is not a spelling variant or clerical error — it is a direct statement about who each man's father was:

- **Lars Eriksen** = Lars, son of a man named **Erik**
- **Lars Pedersen** = Lars, son of a man named **Peder**

Two different patronymics almost certainly mean **two different fathers**, which strongly indicates these are **two different men** — both named Lars, perhaps living in the same parish or region. This was very common, as given names like Lars appeared repeatedly in every community.

---

## How to Confirm Which Scenario You Have

Do not try to match these two records to one person based on the given name alone. Instead, look at:

1. **Farm name (*gårdsname*):** Norwegian farm names were far more stable than patronymics. If both Larses are associated with the **same farm**, they could be the same person — and you'd want to investigate whether one patronymic was recorded in error. If they are associated with **different farms**, you have strong evidence for two distinct individuals.

2. **Parish and geographic location:** Which parish did each record come from? Two different Larses in nearby parishes is simply the expected landscape of Norwegian genealogy.

3. **Dates and life events:** Do the dates overlap in a way that could belong to one person's life, or do they clearly point to two separate lifetimes?

4. **Baptism records:** Parish baptism registers name both the child and the father explicitly. If you find a baptism for "Lars son of Erik" and a separate baptism for "Lars son of Peder" in the same parish around the same period, you have confirmed two distinct individuals.

### Population explosion and what it means for your research

The census data for Schuylkill County tells a striking story: the population more than doubled in a single decade, from 29,053 in 1840 to 60,713 in 1850, then grew to 89,510 by 1860. That rate of growth was driven almost entirely by coal-driven immigration. For your research, this means your ancestor was part of an enormous incoming population — which is both good news (many records were created to manage this population) and a challenge (common names like Jones or Murphy appear hundreds of times in the same county).

### The ethnic workforce — who was there in the 1850s and why it matters

According to Wikipedia's article on the anthracite coal region, the workforce in the 1850s was predominantly two groups:

**Welsh miners** arrived from the 1820s through the 1840s, drawing on expertise from the hard-coal mines of South Wales. They came first and tended to hold skilled and supervisory positions — mine foremen, shot-firers, company weighmen. If your ancestor was Welsh, he may appear in church records written entirely in the Welsh language. Welsh surnames (Jones, Evans, Williams, Thomas, Davis) were so common in the region that miners were often distinguished by occupation or neighborhood even in informal records.

**Irish Catholic miners**, many of whom fled the Great Famine (1845–1852), arrived in large numbers just before and during the 1850s and filled the unskilled and semi-skilled labor roles — haulers, laborers on the surface, and eventually contract miners underground. If your ancestor was Irish, he was likely part of one of the Catholic parishes established in the patch towns throughout the 1840s and 1860s.

The later waves of Southern and Eastern European immigrants — Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Ukrainians — came primarily from the 1870s onward, so they are unlikely to be relevant to a 1850s ancestor unless that ancestor lived into the later period.

### "Patch towns" — the geography of coal mining records

The anthracite region was organized around individual collieries and their associated "patch towns" — company-owned villages built directly adjacent to mine shafts. Each colliery had its own patch, and each patch typically had its own church, company store, and social organizations. **Knowing which colliery or patch your ancestor worked at is the most important geographic fact for finding his records.** The same county, the same decade, but different patches mean different churches, different employers, and different surviving records.

### Record types and where to find them

**Company records** are potentially the most direct evidence of your ancestor's employment. Anthracite coal companies maintained colliery payroll books, time ledgers, and company store account books at the mine level. Where they survive, they are held at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville), the Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, Delaware), and the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg). Company store ledger entries can establish where and when an ancestor worked even when other records are absent.

**Mine inspector reports** were filed annually from 1870 onward and can document workforce size, national origin of employees, and accidents. These are valuable for a later period and may help trace an ancestor who was working in the 1850s and continued into the 1870s.

**Welsh church records**: Welsh immigrants established Calvinist Methodist and Congregational chapels in nearly every patch town by the 1840s. The baptism, marriage, and burial registers were kept in Welsh. Many survive at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and at the Welsh Presbyterian Church archives. FamilySearch has digitized copies catalogued under "Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Church Records." If your ancestor was Welsh, be aware that the records may require translation from Welsh.

**Irish Catholic church records**: St. Patrick's Church in Pottsville was founded in 1827, and dozens of later parishes served the patch towns throughout the 1840s–1860s. Many of these registers are digitized on FamilySearch under "Pennsylvania, Catholic Church Records." The Diocese of Harrisburg (separated from Philadelphia in 1868) holds the majority of surviving registers for Schuylkill County parishes; for records before 1868, check the Diocese of Philadelphia.

Miners in the same ethnic community socialized, worshipped, and often witnessed records for each other. output.text_response:
Your ancestor almost certainly did **not** move. This is a classic boundary-change situation, and the two census entries are entirely consistent with one another.

---

## What Happened Between 1860 and 1870

West Virginia was admitted to the Union as the 35th state on **20 June 1863**, carved directly out of the state of Virginia. Before that date, the territory that became West Virginia was simply Virginia. So in 1860, any person born in what is now West Virginia was correctly recorded as born in Virginia — because Virginia was the only state that existed there at the time of their birth.

By 1870, census enumerators were recording birthplaces using the **current** political geography. A person born before 1863 in what is now, say, Kanawha County would now be said to have been born in "West Virginia" — even though that state did not exist on the day of their birth. The enumerator (or the ancestor reporting the information) used the name of the state as it then existed, not as it existed at the time of the birth.

---

## What the Two Entries Together Actually Tell You

Both census entries describe the **same birthplace**. The 1860 entry reflects the political reality at the time the person was born. The 1870 entry reflects the political reality at the time the census was taken. Neither entry is wrong. Neither signals a move.

---

## Research Implications

Because your ancestor was born in what is now West Virginia but was then Virginia, pre-1863 records about the family — deeds, court records, tax lists, church records, probate — will be **filed under Virginia**, specifically in whichever Virginia county contained that location before the split. After June 1863, records fall under West Virginia.

The key next step is to identify the **specific county** your ancestor lived in:
- For records **before 1863**, search in the Virginia predecessor county.
- For records **from 1863 onward**, search in the West Virginia county.

---

*Source consulted: [West Virginia, United States Genealogy – FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/West_Virginia,_United_States_Genealogy)*
